In ML, this means establishing clear, quantifiable performance metrics at the outset of the project. These metrics provide an objective and rigorous standard for comparing different models and for determining whether a model is performing well enough to be deployed. Throughout the five case studies, metrics such as root mean squared error (RMSE), which measures the average magnitude of a model's prediction errors, were used consistently to provide a quantifiable assessment of model performance. By defining what "good" looks like in numerical terms, the project teams could move beyond subjective assessments and make data-driven decisions about which modeling approaches were most effective. 2.5.3 Pillar 3: Interpretability One of the most significant barriers to the adoption of advanced ML models is the "black box" problem. Complex models like neural networks or large ensembles can be opaque, making it difficult for operators and engineers to understand why a particular prediction or recommendation was made. This lack of transparency can erode trust, which is a non- negotiable prerequisite for integrating a new tool into a critical process control loop. To build this trust, it is essential to open the black box. Modern model interpretability tools can illuminate the inner workings of complex models. A leading example used in this project is SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis (Lundberg and Lee 2017). SHAP is a sophisticated method, grounded in cooperative game theory, that assigns an importance value to each input 18 The Water Research Foundation feature for every individual prediction, showing how much each factor pushed the prediction higher or lower (Lundberg and Lee 2017). The application of SHAP in the carbon diversion (Application 1) and disinfection (Application 3) case studies was highlighted as being crucial for building the operational confidence needed for deployment. By providing clear, visual explanations for model behavior, these tools transform a model from an inscrutable oracle into a transparent and trustworthy analytical partner (Lundberg and Lee 2017). 2.5.4 Pillar 4: Human-in-the-Loop The final, and arguably most important, pillar is the human element. A recurring theme throughout this project's lessons learned is that ML is a tool to empower engineers and operators, not replace them. The successful deployment of a data-driven solution is not simply a technical handoff from data scientists to operations. Rather, it is the outcome of a deeply collaborative effort where operators and other stakeholders are engaged throughout the entire process—from initial problem definition to final deployment and ongoing monitoring. This continuous engagement builds institutional knowledge, fosters trust, and ensures that the final tool is not only technically sound but also practical, useful, and integrated into the existing operational culture.
